How Kansas property tax is calculated

A Kansas tax bill comes in two steps. The county appraiser's estimate of fair market value, multiplied by an assessment rate, gives the assessed value. Take that assessed figure, apply the mill levy, and divide by 1,000 to arrive at the tax.

The residential assessment rate is 11.5%. Commercial property is assessed at 25% of full value. One mill means $1 in tax on every $1,000 of assessed value. The levy stacks up the rates of every local taxing body, such as the school district, county and city. The county clerk can tell you the levy for your address.

The state's own teaching example uses a $200,000 home and a combined levy of 130 mills. Treat that as an illustration of the method, not a forecast for any particular house.

Property tax calendar

A Kansas tax year opens with valuation notices by March 1 and closes with the second-half payment on May 10 of the next year. Sellers and owners should watch the dates below.

Kansas property tax calendar for real estate
DateEvent
March 1County sends valuation notices
30 days from mailingFinal day to start an equalization appeal with the county appraiser
May 15Deadline for the informal meeting with the appraiser
May 20Appraiser issues the final determination
June 1Appraiser sends certified values to the clerk
August 25Budgets go to the clerk from each governing body
November 1Clerk hands the tax roll to the treasurer
December 20Payment in full, or the first half, is due
May 10Second half comes due

Personal property runs on a separate schedule, and its valuation notices are dated May 1. If you sell a house that includes a mobile home, a boat or business equipment, ask the county which schedule each item falls under.

What to check on your valuation notice

The notice that arrives by March 1 is your only cheap chance to challenge the number. Read the appraised value first and ask whether it matches what similar homes near you would sell for. Then look at the dates, because the clock for an equalization appeal starts on the mailing date printed on the notice, not the day it reaches your mailbox.

If the value looks high, call the county appraiser before the informal meeting date and ask what data supports it. Bring photos of any damage, repair estimates, and a recent appraisal if you have one. A seller with an old roof or a cracked foundation has a better case when the paperwork is in the file.

Who sets the mill levy

Every taxing unit writes its own levy from its budget. The revenue neutral rate is the mill levy that, applied to the current year's assessed valuation, would produce the same property tax revenue as the prior year.

Public steps are built into the calendar around it. The county clerk reports the rate for each taxing jurisdiction by June 15. A governing body that wants to go above it tells the county clerk by July 20 and holds a public hearing between August 20 and September 20. That hearing window is the best time for a homeowner to speak up about a rising bill, because budgets are certified by August 25.

The levy is one reason two houses with the same appraised value can carry different bills. A house in one school district or city can sit under a higher combined levy than a house a few blocks away in another. Buyers compare tax bills across neighborhoods, so learn your own levy before you settle on an asking price. Your county clerk can give you the number, and your last tax statement shows what you paid.

How to appeal your valuation

You have two routes, and for a given tax year you must choose one: an equalization appeal after the spring notice, or payment under protest when you pay.

  • Equalization appeal: call the county appraiser within a month of the date the notice was mailed, then go to the informal meeting, which must happen by May 15.
  • Third-party appraisal option: after the informal result, the owner may file a fee simple appraisal done by a Kansas certified appraiser inside 60 days after the notice went out. The county then has 90 days to respond.
  • Payment under protest: hand the protest form to the county treasurer at the time you pay. December 20 is the cutoff, even if you are paying only the first half.

An informal meeting that fails to settle things sends you on to the Board of Tax Appeals. Single-family homes go to the BOTA Small Claims Division first. So does any non-agricultural property valued under $3 million. One hearing officer hears small claims appeals, and the appeal form usually comes with the notice of informal meeting results. Each filing deadline is 30 days after the earlier decision was mailed.

What happens when the tax goes unpaid

Unpaid Kansas real estate tax draws interest and, after enough time, can lead to a county foreclosure sale. K.S.A. 79-2004 gives two choices: pay it all by December 20, or pay half then and half on May 10. Weekend deadlines roll forward to Monday or the next business day. Tiny bills of $10 or less cannot be split and are due whole on December 20.

Miss the first half and interest starts at the K.S.A. 79-2968 rate, with five percentage points added each year. Any balance left after May 10 keeps drawing that same rate, and the meter runs until you pay or the county forecloses and sells the property.

Foreclosure comes later. Under K.S.A. 79-2801, when property the county bought at sale remains unredeemed on September 1 of the second year afterward, the county attorney is directed to file an action in district court. The law makes that action discretionary where the aggregate assessed valuation is under $300,000 or the delinquent taxes and special assessments are under $10,000. If the county does not act on property inside a city and the taxes have stayed delinquent for three years after the property became eligible, the city may start the foreclosure itself.

If a delinquency notice has already arrived, read it closely and call the county treasurer right away about redemption. Waiting costs money, because interest keeps building every year the balance sits open, and a sale that is still weeks away can be derailed by a lien nobody planned for.

If you owe tax when you sell

The closing agent normally pays the current year's tax plus any arrears from your sale proceeds. Because a tax lien stays with the property, it must be cleared before a buyer can take clean title. Get a payoff number from the title company well ahead of closing day.

  • The recorded deed must show the buyer's name and mailing address. The register of deeds passes that address to the county clerk so tax statements reach the right person (K.S.A. 58-2221).
  • A deed generally needs a sales validation questionnaire. K.S.A. 79-1437f keeps sale prices off the public record.
  • Questions about a specific property's value belong with the county appraiser, and the county treasurer answers payment questions.

If a house has delinquent taxes, a repair backlog or a probate hold, our team can look at it as-is. A title company will ask about the same tax points, so have your latest tax statement in hand when you call.

Before you list, collect the newest valuation notice and tax statement, confirm what has been paid, and find out whether an appeal or protest is still open.

Frequently asked questions

When are Kansas property taxes due?

Real estate tax is due in full by December 20, or in two halves with the first by December 20 and the second by May 10 of the next year (K.S.A. 79-2004). A due date on a weekend moves to the next business day.

How long do I have to appeal my Kansas valuation?

Thirty days from the date the county mailed the notice of value. The notice goes out by March 1, so the window usually closes in spring. The informal meeting with the county appraiser must be held by May 15.

Can I appeal and also pay under protest?

No. A taxpayer picks one path for the same tax year: appeal at the valuation notice or pay under protest, not both.

What is the residential assessment rate in Kansas?

Residential property is assessed at 11.5% of appraised value. The assessed value is then multiplied by the combined mill levy and divided by 1,000 to produce the tax.

Who do I contact about my Kansas property tax bill?

The county appraiser handles value questions, the county clerk holds the mill levy, and the county treasurer takes payments and the payment under protest form.

What the Kansas homestead exemption covers

Kansans use the word homestead for three different things: protection from forced sale by creditors, a yearly refund of part of the property tax, and a school-levy break on the first slice of a home's value. Only the first is a true exemption. The other two run through different agencies.

The constitutional protection sits in Article 15, Section 9 of the Kansas Constitution and is repeated in K.S.A. 60-2301. It covers up to 160 acres of farm land, or one acre inside an incorporated town or city, or a manufactured or mobile home, occupied as a residence by the owner or the owner's family. Improvements on the land are included.

The Department of Revenue runs the tax refund. The school-levy exemption comes from the state property tax statutes and is handled by the Property Valuation Division. A seller who wants to know what a sale does to each of these has to look at them one at a time.

Kansas homestead numbers at a glance

Homestead ruleAmount or limit
Forced-sale protection (K.S.A. 60-2301)160 acres of farm land or 1 acre within a city
Homestead refund (K-40H) income limit$43,389 or less for tax year 2025
Maximum property tax counted$700
Property valued over$350,000 does not qualify
K-40PT senior refundAge 65 or older, income $25,380 or less, 75% of tax paid
K-40SVR income limit$58,041
Filing windowOpens after December 31 of the tax year and closes April 15 of the next year
School-levy exemptionFirst $75,000 of appraised value, 20 mill statewide levy

Can a creditor force the sale of a Kansas homestead?

Generally no, with a few written exceptions. A qualifying homestead is exempt from forced sale under any process of law. No property is exempt from sale for taxes, or for debts contracted to buy the property or to build improvements on it.

The protection also doesn't reach a lien given with the consent of both spouses, when the owner is married. That is why a mortgage can still be foreclosed even though the home is a homestead.

If a levy is made on land whose homestead has never been set apart, K.S.A. 60-2302 lets the householder, the spouse, or an agent or attorney give the officer a written notice describing what they regard as the homestead. That notice can come when the levy is made or at any time before the sale, and only the remainder can be sold.

For an owner behind on payments, the point is narrow. The home is shielded from forced sale in general, but taxes, purchase-money debts, improvement debts and liens both spouses agreed to are carved out.

Selling a homestead: spousal consent

When the owner is married, both spouses must agree. A homestead cannot be alienated without the joint consent of husband and wife where that relation exists (K.S.A. 60-2301).

K.S.A. 60-2303 adds a rule about contracts. A suit for specific performance of a contract to sell a homestead, or for damages for breaking such a contract, can't be maintained unless both spouses signed, or an agent or broker authorized in writing by both did. This section does not apply to mortgages.

Practical steps for a married seller:

  • Have both spouses sign the sale contract, even if only one name is on the title.
  • If one spouse is unavailable, ask a Kansas attorney who can sign for them.
  • Keep a written authorization if an agent will sign.

These rules protect the family living in the home. They also mean a buyer will want both signatures in hand before closing.

Who qualifies for the homestead property tax refund?

The K-40H refund is for people who own and occupy a Kansas home and lived in Kansas for the whole tax year. Renters don't qualify. A name on the deed or a contract for deed counts as ownership, while a rent-to-own contract does not.

A household with total income of $43,389 or less qualifies if at least one of these is true:

  • The claimant was born before January 1, 1970.
  • The claimant was blind, totally and permanently disabled, or a disabled veteran for all of 2025.
  • A dependent child under 18 lived with the claimant all year.

Only one claim can be filed per household. Household income counts most taxable and nontaxable income, but only half of Social Security and SSI benefits on the K-40H, and Social Security disability payments are left out. The year-specific limits above are for tax year 2025, so check the current booklet for the year you file.

How the refund is figured and paid

The refund is a percentage of the general property tax paid, with a ceiling on the tax counted. The percentage depends on income: 100 percent at $6,000 or less, 50 percent for incomes from $17,001 to $18,000, 10 percent for $25,001 to $26,000, and 5 percent for incomes from $26,001 up to the $43,389 limit. Income of $43,390 or more gets nothing.

The tax counted is the lower of the tax billed or $700, and taxes on property valued at more than $350,000 don't qualify. Special assessments, service charges and late interest are left out. A refund under $5 is not paid.

Two property tax installments are in play, due December 20 and May 10, and the K-40H counts both whether or not they have been paid. Complete paper claims take about 20 to 24 weeks to process.

If the home carries delinquent property tax, the Department of Revenue sends the whole refund to the county treasurer. A refund can also be taken for other debts owed to the state.

Late claims can be accepted for good cause if filed within four years of the original due date. An optional Refund Advancement Program applies part of an expected refund to the first-half tax bill.

Refunds when a home is sold or the owner dies

A homeowner who moved during the year can claim the general property tax paid for the time lived in each residence. One who rented out part of the house can claim only the tax on the part they lived in, worked out by the share of rooms rented or used for business.

When an owner has died, another qualifying member of the household files for the household. If no household member qualifies, a claim can be filed for the deceased claimant if they lived in Kansas for the part of the year they were alive. The refund is prorated by the month of death, from 8.3 percent for January up to 100 percent for December. The claim needs a death certificate, funeral home notice or obituary, plus letters of administration if the estate is in probate or Form RF-9 if it is not.

Heirs who inherit a Kansas house often find the property tax bill, not the refund, is the first deadline. Estimated real estate taxes prorated for the year of sale are a normal escrow closing cost, so the split between seller and buyer is usually settled at closing.

If you are selling, ask the title company how the tax proration will be shown on the settlement statement, and keep your tax bills so you can claim the refund for the months you owned the house.

The $75,000 school levy exemption

For tax year 2024 and every year after, the first $75,000 of appraised value of residential property is exempt from the statewide school finance levy. The exemption is limited to the 20 mill school district levy.

The figure comes from Senate Bill 1 of the 2024 special session, which stopped the earlier formula that raised the amount each year by the average statewide increase in value. Because the amount is fixed, it helps a lower-priced home proportionally more than an expensive one.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Kansas homestead exemption the same as the homestead refund?

No. The exemption in Article 15, Section 9 and K.S.A. 60-2301 protects a home from forced sale. The K-40H refund is a partial property tax rebate that the Department of Revenue pays on a claim.

How much is the Kansas homestead refund?

The maximum counted is $700 of general property tax, with the percentage based on household income. Taxes on property valued above $350,000 don't qualify.

When do I file a Kansas homestead claim?

After December 31 of the tax year and no later than April 15 of the next year. Late claims can be accepted for good cause within four years of the original due date.

Do both spouses have to sign to sell a Kansas homestead?

Yes. Under K.S.A. 60-2301 and 60-2303, a homestead can't be alienated without the joint consent of the spouses, and a suit to enforce a sale contract needs both signatures or an agent they authorized in writing.

Can I get the homestead refund if I rent out part of my house?

Yes, but only for the part you live in. A room-count worksheet sets the share, and rental income is reported on the claim.

Kansas estate tax and inheritance tax

If the owner died after December 31, 2009, Kansas collects no estate tax. Lawmakers wrote no estate tax provisions for those deaths, so nothing is owed, and the Department of Revenue turns away returns filed for them.

That history is why outdated advice lingers. An estate tax took the place of the old inheritance tax in 1998, covering deaths on or after July 1, 1998. The version covering deaths after December 31, 2006 and before January 1, 2010 sits at K.S.A. 79-15,201 and following, and K.S.A. 79-15,253 repealed it on January 1, 2010.

For a recent death the state-level question is settled. What's left is the federal estate tax and income tax on any gain once the house is sold.

When the federal estate tax reaches a Kansas house

Only for a very large estate. A 2026 death carries a basic exclusion amount of $15,000,000.

Federal figure2026 amount
Basic exclusion amount (year of death)$15,000,000
Credit equivalent at 2026 rates$5,945,800
Yearly gift exclusion, each recipient$19,000

That figure adds up everything the person owned, so a Kansas family home is usually a small slice. Under the exclusion, federal estate tax plays no role in a keep-or-sell decision.

Basis for an heir

For an heir, basis is generally what the house was worth on the day of death (IRS Publication 551). Newer guidance covers certain property whose basis must match the value finally reported for estate tax.

Timing therefore drives the income tax bill. A sale near the value at death produces a small gain, while years of appreciation enlarge it. An appraisal as of the death date is cheap insurance against a basis dispute later. The sale then falls under the rules on our Kansas capital gains page.

There is one exception. Appreciated property that you or your spouse gave the decedent within a year of death comes back to you with the decedent's adjusted basis instead.

Probate before selling an inherited Kansas house

A house titled only in the decedent's name generally can't be sold until a court names someone to act. The case is normally opened in the county where the property sits, and the executor or administrator reports to the District Court.

  • Six months: file the petition to open probate no later than 6 months after the person died.
  • Four to five weeks: typical wait for an executor's appointment once the petition is in.
  • Four months: creditors have 4 months after actual notice to file claims.
  • Six months again: an estate with assets left after allowances and debts can't close earlier than 6 months after death.

The executor lists and safeguards assets, pays valid creditor claims (selling property if needed) and hands out the remainder. Acting on a dead person's property without appointment can make you personally liable. Wait to list, repair or remove anything until an attorney confirms who has authority.

Property that skips probate

Some assets pass outside the will: real estate in joint tenancy with right of survivorship, real estate titled in transfer on death form, life insurance, and pay on death accounts.

Transfer on death deeds are governed by K.S.A. 59-3501 and following. The owner names a beneficiary in a deed that must be executed, acknowledged and recorded with the register of deeds where the land sits while the owner is alive (K.S.A. 59-3502). At the owner's death, title vests in the beneficiary (K.S.A. 59-3504). Recording in Johnson County runs $21 for the first page and $17 for each additional page.

If there was no will and the estate is only real estate, a Determination of Descent can be started any time after 6 months from death. It usually wraps up in about 30 days.

Property tax while the estate is open

Probate doesn't pause the tax bills, and the county keeps mailing them. In Johnson County, the treasurer collects either in full by December 20 or in two halves, due December 20 and May 10, with interest on late payments under K.S.A. 79-2004. A bill you never received doesn't stop interest.

There, tax still unpaid by July 31 is published in the newspaper with a $15 fee, a lien attaches on the first Tuesday in September, and a foreclosure suit follows if the redemption period runs out. Procedures differ by county, so call the treasurer where the house stands. If the executor pays from estate funds, a future buyer gets clean title.

Paying taxes and debts on time is part of the executor's duty, so rank the tax bill above cosmetic repairs.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Kansas houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How an estate sale differs at closing

A sale out of an estate has a few extra stops that an ordinary listing lacks. The buyer's title company wants to see the document that gives the seller power to sign, whether that is court letters, a recorded beneficiary deed or a death certificate paired with a joint tenancy deed. Any lender with a mortgage on the house must be paid off from the proceeds, and the tax account must be current.

Where several heirs share the house, all of them, or the executor on their behalf, have to agree on price and terms. A single holdout can stall the deal for months. Talk through the plan as a family before a contract is signed, and write down who is responsible for utilities and insurance in the meantime.

After closing, the proceeds go to the estate or directly to the heirs, depending on the court's instructions. Keep the settlement statement, because it supports the sale price used when the gain is figured.

A practical order of steps for heirs

Work in this order: establish who has authority, check the tax account, and only then choose between holding and selling.

  • Learn how title is held: transfer on death deed, joint tenancy, or the probate estate.
  • Call the county treasurer about the tax account, because unpaid tax earns interest and can end in foreclosure.
  • Get a date-of-death value in writing for your basis records.
  • Keep insurance active and the doors locked until the court process ends.
  • If probate applies, list only after the personal representative has written court authority.

Heirs who live far away, or who inherit a house that needs work, sometimes pick a direct as-is sale to stop paying taxes, utilities and upkeep while probate runs. The choice is yours, and the legal steps are the same either way. Cash buyers still ask for proof of authority, clear title and a paid-up tax account, so having those on hand shortens any closing. Bring the letters from the court, the deed, recent tax statements and the date-of-death value to your first meeting with a buyer or attorney.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a Kansas inheritance tax on a house I inherit?

No Kansas death tax applies to anyone who died after December 31, 2009. The Department of Revenue won't process estate tax returns for those deaths.

What is the federal estate tax exemption for 2026?

For a 2026 death the federal basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000, and smaller estates generally owe nothing.

Do I need probate before selling an inherited Kansas house?

Often, when the house was in the decedent's name alone. Joint tenancy property and houses under a recorded transfer on death deed skip probate.

How long do I have to open probate in Kansas?

No later than 6 months after death. An executor is typically appointed 4 to 5 weeks after the petition is filed.

What is my tax basis in an inherited house?

Usually its market value when the owner died, unless you or your spouse gave it to the deceased within a year before death.

How a Kansas eviction begins

Every Kansas eviction opens with a written notice from the landlord. Only after the notice runs out can the landlord ask a judge for possession. Neither the notice nor the courthouse can be skipped.

The reason for the eviction sets the notice. For unpaid rent, K.S.A. 58-2564 lets the landlord terminate the rental agreement if the tenant hasn't paid within three days of written notice, counted as three consecutive 24-hour periods. Mailing adds two days. The notice can be handed to the tenant, handed to someone over 12 years old who lives there, or posted in a conspicuous place on the premises.

A lease breach unrelated to rent gets a notice describing the problem. The tenant has 14 days to fix it, and if the problem remains, the agreement ends no sooner than 30 days after the notice is received. A similar breach later on can bring a 30-day termination notice with no second chance to cure.

One practical point: a separate three-day notice to leave must also precede filing, although a single document can do double duty as the termination notice and the notice to leave.

Court steps and timing

A typical Kansas eviction case can take up to 42 days from petition to writ. The landlord files in the district court of the county where the house sits.

StepWhat happensTiming
PetitionLandlord files; may add a claim for unpaid rentHearing set 3 to 14 days after filing
SummonsTenant is served and must answer in writing or appearOn or before the hearing date
Bench trialJudge hears both sides if the tenant contestsWithin 14 days of the hearing date
JudgmentJudge rules on possessionAt or after trial
Writ of restitutionSheriff or process server removes the tenantExecuted within 14 days

The governing statutes are K.S.A. 61-3801 through 61-3808, and the Kansas Judicial Branch self-help page walks through the process. A tenant who misses the first date risks a default judgment, which gives the landlord everything the petition asked for.

A tenant who loses may be ordered out quickly, in some cases within 24 hours. For anyone planning a sale around a vacant house, the writ date is the deadline that counts.

What a landlord can never do

Changing the locks, cutting off utilities or otherwise forcing a tenant out without a court order is off limits. K.S.A. 58-2569 bars a landlord from taking possession by action or by interrupting electric, gas, water or other essential service, with exceptions for abandonment or surrender.

Forcible removal belongs to the people authorized to carry out a writ of restitution. A tenant who is locked out or shut off may be able to sue in small claims court for up to one and one-half months of rent, or for damages if that is greater, potentially including punitive damages.

Owners selling a rented house sometimes feel pressure to speed things up. Shortcuts can create a claim against the owner that outlives the sale.

Belongings a tenant leaves behind

Kansas sets a defined path for abandoned belongings:

  • The landlord can store the property at the tenant's cost, sell it or dispose of it, but not until 30 days after taking possession.
  • Notice must be published in a newspaper in the county, giving the tenant's name, a description of the items and the disposal date.
  • A copy of the notice is mailed to the tenant's last known address.
  • The tenant can claim the items within the 30 days by paying storage, publication and similar costs.

Sale proceeds go first to storage costs and then to other debts the tenant owes. When a house has to be emptied before closing, this step most often delays the handoff to a buyer.

County programs that help avoid trial

Three of the largest counties run programs through their district courts.

  • Douglas County: an Eviction Resolution Program with a coordinator who connects both sides to rental assistance, legal aid and mediation.
  • Johnson County: an Eviction Mediation Program where a neutral mediator helps the parties reach an agreement before trial.
  • Sedgwick County: an Eviction Resolution Program that explains the court process and points to financial help, legal aid, mediation and emergency housing.

A landlord who plans to sell can use these programs to settle on a move-out date by agreement. A signed agreement with a firm date is often easier on a buyer than a contested case.

Former tenants have one more option. Some Kansas eviction cases can now be expunged, removing the court record from public view (2026 Substitute for House Bill 2357), and the courts run an online portal for people who file without a lawyer.

When the occupant is not a tenant

The residential landlord and tenant act doesn't cover someone who enters and stays with no rental agreement and without the landlord's knowledge, knowing they have no right to be there, after the landlord has personally told them to leave. Under K.S.A. 58-2573 such a person may be prosecuted for criminal trespass.

Where no landlord-tenant relationship exists and no other notice period applies, notice must be delivered at least three days before the petition is filed. Criminal trespass is a class B nonperson misdemeanor, with up to six months in county jail, a fine up to $1,000, or both. Only a county or district attorney, or a city prosecutor under a city ordinance, can bring those charges.

Kansas adverse possession takes 15 years of open, exclusive and continuous possession under K.S.A. 60-503, so an unwanted occupant of a few months has no ownership claim. The owner still has to use the eviction process or the trespass route rather than self-help.

Selling a rented Kansas house during an eviction

Selling a rented house doesn't end the tenant's rights, and an eviction in progress doesn't stop a sale. Under K.S.A. 58-2554, a landlord who sells in a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability under the rental agreement for events after written notice of the sale goes to the tenant. The seller stays liable for any part of the security deposit the tenant is owed.

The deposit catches owners off guard. If you sell with the tenant in place, it doesn't vanish at closing, so the closing paperwork should say who holds it and who answers to the tenant.

Owners in this spot usually weigh three paths:

  • Finish the eviction first and hand over a vacant house, accepting the notice and court timeline above.
  • Sell with the tenant in place and give the written notice the statute describes.
  • Negotiate a move-out with the tenant, using a county mediation program if one exists.

Cash Home Buyers buys houses as-is, including some with tenants or damage left behind. Tell us what stage the case is in and we can talk through which path fits. A Kansas attorney should confirm the legal steps for your file.

Official forms and help

The Kansas Judicial Council publishes eviction forms with instruction sheets for landlords and for tenants who respond. The nonpayment instructions tell the landlord to complete a civil cover sheet, mark the landlord and tenant forcible detainer category, and submit an eviction summons to the clerk. Service can be by sheriff, process server or return receipt delivery, and the clerk quotes the filing fee unless the filer submits an affidavit of inability to pay.

Kansas Legal Services runs an intake line at 316-267-3975. The self-help page also lists the Kansas Housing Resource Corporation, 211 Kansas and HUD resources for people who need rental help.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a landlord have to wait after a three-day notice in Kansas?

Three days, counted as three consecutive 24-hour periods under K.S.A. 58-2564, plus two more if the notice is mailed. The landlord can then file a petition in district court.

How long does a Kansas eviction take once it is filed?

Up to 42 days is typical. The hearing is set within 3 to 14 days of filing, a trial within 14 days of that hearing, and the writ is executed within 14 days.

Can a Kansas landlord evict by shutting off the water or changing the locks?

No. K.S.A. 58-2569 prohibits it, and a tenant may be able to sue for up to one and one-half months of rent or damages.

Can I sell my Kansas rental while an eviction is pending?

Yes, nothing in the statutes bars it. Under K.S.A. 58-2554 the seller is relieved of later liability only after written notice of the sale goes to the tenant, and still owes any deposit the tenant is entitled to.

Can a Kansas eviction record be removed?

Some eviction cases can now be expunged under 2026 Substitute for House Bill 2357. The courts provide an online portal for people who represent themselves.

What a quitclaim deed does in Kansas

With a quitclaim, the signer passes along whatever share of the land they hold, and promises nothing about its quality. K.S.A. 58-2204 gives the short form: "A.B. quitclaims to C.D.," followed by the description of the premises and the consideration, signed and acknowledged by the grantor.

Compare it with a warranty deed. A warranty deed is the seller's guarantee that title is clean and that earlier owners or heirs hold no claim. A quitclaim simply releases the name of someone who may have an interest. That is why quitclaims show up between family members, after a divorce or when co-owners shuffle names, and why a buyer in an ordinary sale usually asks for a warranty deed.

What the register of deeds needs before recording

A deed has to name both parties, describe the land, carry a proper notary acknowledgment and come with a sales validation questionnaire or a stated exemption. Johnson County and Wyandotte County apply nearly identical rules, which follow the statutes (K.S.A. 58-2205, 58-2209, 58-2211, 58-2221).

  • The grantor's name, the grantee's name and the legal description of the property.
  • Signatures that are properly notarized, with the full date, the notary's appointment expiration date and the state and county where the act took place.
  • A notary certificate with no blanks, the notary's seal and a signer name that matches the name in the deed.
  • Page one with a 3-inch top margin and 1-inch margins on the other three sides, with 1-inch margins on every later page, on letter-size paper.
  • The full name and mailing address of the person receiving the property, which the register forwards to the county clerk for tax statements.

Johnson County cannot accept a document for recording by email or fax. Bring it in person, mail it with a return envelope or use an approved electronic recording vendor. If a document misses the margin rules, K.S.A. 28-115 lets the register add a sheet for the recording information or copy the document, and those extra pages are charged. Illegible documents can be rejected.

Sales validation questionnaire and exemptions

Usually a questionnaire is required, unless one of the statutory exemptions applies and the deed says so. K.S.A. 79-1437c bars recording of a deed that arrives without the questionnaire, and K.S.A. 79-1437e lists the exempt transfers. An exemption must be clearly stated on the document being filed. The register cannot add it for you.

Transfers exempt from the questionnaire under K.S.A. 79-1437e
Exempt transferTypical quitclaim use
Gift, donation or contribution stated in the deedFamily transfer with no payment
Divorce settlementOne spouse deeds out to the other
Solely to create a joint tenancy or tenancy in commonOwner adds a co-owner
To or from a trust without considerationMoving a house into or out of a trust
Quitclaim filed to clear title encumbrancesClearing a cloud on title
Correcting a recorded deed with no added considerationFixing a name or description
Transfer by a fiduciary under judicial orderExecutor or conservator conveyance

What a buyer paid stays out of the public record (K.S.A. 79-1437f). The questionnaires are kept for five years and are not filed of record.

Recording fees

State law (K.S.A. 28-115) sets recording fees, and each register's office posts the totals. In Wyandotte County a deed costs $21 for page one and $17 for every page after it. Plain copies are $1 per page, with $13 more for a certified copy.

Each county posts its own schedule. Phone the register where the property is located before mailing a check. Wyandotte requires payment in advance for copy requests, and its recording desk takes checks payable to the Register of Deeds. Johnson County accepts walk-ins on weekdays, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

These fees cover recording only. A lawyer's time or a title company's charges are separate, so budget for them if you want help preparing the deed.

When a quitclaim makes sense, and when it does not

A quitclaim works best when everyone already agrees who should hold title and nobody needs a guarantee. It is a poor fit when someone is paying for the property and expects clean title.

  • Good fit: putting a spouse or relative on or off the title, moving a house into a trust, releasing a possible claim of a former co-owner.
  • Works poorly: a sale to a buyer who will ask for a warranty deed, or a transfer meant to settle a dispute about ownership that has not actually been resolved.
  • Cannot do: change a recorded document. A recorded deed is a permanent record, so any change to the title requires a new document to be prepared and recorded.

Register staff cannot draft your deed or advise you on the wording. Use a lawyer or a title company, though a person is allowed to make out their own deed. Wyandotte posts blank sample forms for a general quitclaim deed and a joint tenancy quitclaim deed on its website.

Selling a house after a quitclaim deed

Once the recorded deed shows the right owners, those owners can sign the sale deed. A quitclaim often comes first in family situations. Heirs deed the house among themselves, or a parent deeds it to a child, and then the new owner decides to sell.

Check three things before listing or taking an offer. First, confirm the quitclaim was recorded in the county where the house sits, because K.S.A. 58-2221 sends recording to that county's register of deeds. Second, confirm the mortgage and tax balances, since a deed changes ownership on the record and does not remove either. Third, if the house came to you through a death, read our pages on the Kansas probate process and the transfer on death deed, because a court order or an earlier TOD deed may control who can sign.

We buy Kansas houses as-is, including homes where the title paperwork is still being sorted out. A title company will review the recorded deeds before closing, so having your quitclaim and its recording stamp ready speeds up that review.

Avoiding deed fraud

Check recorded documents and keep a copy of anything you sign. Fake or forced deeds are a recognized problem, and Wyandotte County posts a property fraud alert in English and Spanish that links to PropertyFraudAlert.com. A quitclaim moves ownership without a warranty, so be wary of anyone who asks you to sign one quickly, and have a lawyer look at it first.

Steps to record your own quitclaim

Start with the current deed so you can copy the legal description exactly. Prepare the new deed with both names and the grantee's mailing address, then sign it in front of a notary. Complete the sales validation questionnaire or write the exemption into the deed. Finally, take the packet to the register of deeds in the county where the land sits and pay the recording fee.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Kansas statute for a quitclaim deed?

K.S.A. 58-2204 sets out the short form, "A.B. quitclaims to C.D.," with a description of the premises and the consideration, signed and acknowledged by the grantor. Recording is handled under K.S.A. 58-2221.

Where do I record a quitclaim deed in Kansas?

With the register of deeds in the county where the land is located. In Johnson County that means the office in Olathe, and in Wyandotte County it is at the courthouse in Kansas City, Kansas.

Does a quitclaim deed need to be notarized in Kansas?

Yes. The signature must be acknowledged before a notary, with the full date, the notary's expiration date, the jurisdiction and the notary's seal on the certificate. An incomplete certificate gets the document returned.

Do I need a sales validation questionnaire for a quitclaim?

Usually, unless an exemption in K.S.A. 79-1437e applies, such as a gift stated in the deed or a divorce settlement. If an exemption applies, the deed itself must say so.

Can the register of deeds help me write a quitclaim deed?

No. The register of deeds is a records custodian and can answer general process questions only. Use a lawyer or a title company for drafting.

What a Kansas transfer on death deed is

A transfer on death deed, also called a TOD deed or beneficiary deed, names the person who will receive a piece of real estate when the owner dies. Until then the owner keeps full control. It looks like a regular deed but does not take effect until death. The rules sit in Article 35 of Chapter 59 of the Kansas Statutes, K.S.A. 59-3501 and following.

The roles are simple. The owner is the grantor, the person who will receive the property is the grantee beneficiary, and the deed stays revocable for the owner's whole life. It covers land and homes, and it can also cover certain oil, gas and mineral rights and royalties.

Making a TOD deed valid

The deed has to be signed, acknowledged and recorded with the register of deeds in the county where the property sits, and all of that must happen before the owner dies. K.S.A. 59-3502 supplies the wording: the owner transfers on death to the named beneficiary, followed by the description of the interest. The deed must also say that it is revocable and transfers no ownership until the owner's death. The abbreviation "TOD" may replace the full words.

  • Copy the legal description from your current deed, so get a copy of that deed first.
  • Sign before a notary. Johnson County and Wyandotte County both turn away deeds with incomplete notary certificates.
  • Record it before death. Johnson County's filing rules require a TOD deed to be filed before the grantor dies.
  • Skip the beneficiary's signature. The statute makes the beneficiary's signature, consent or notice unnecessary.

Wyandotte County posts sample forms, including a general TOD deed and a joint tenancy version. Registers cannot draft documents for you. Ask a lawyer or title company when the facts are not straightforward.

What happens when the owner dies

Title passes to the named beneficiary at the moment of the owner's death, and that property needs no probate. Under K.S.A. 59-3504, title to real estate recorded in TOD form vests in the designated grantee beneficiary on the death of the record owner.

The beneficiary takes the house with everything the owner had attached to it. The statute lists conveyances, contracts, mortgages, liens and security pledges, plus any executory contract of sale, option to purchase, lease, easement or deed of trust. It also names claims of the State of Kansas for medical assistance. A TOD deed does not wipe the slate clean.

How a TOD deed works over time
Point in timeWhat the law provides
While the owner is alive (K.S.A. 59-3502, 59-3503)Deed transfers no ownership; owner can sell, revoke or change it
At the owner's death (59-3504(a))Title vests in the grantee beneficiary
After vesting (59-3504(b))Beneficiary takes subject to liens, mortgages, leases and Medicaid claims
If the beneficiary dies first (59-3504(c))Transfer lapses unless an alternate or surviving issue qualifies

The beneficiary usually records a certified death certificate so the public record shows why title moved. The Johnson and Wyandotte registers both take a state-certified copy under K.S.A. 58-501 and 65-2416, with no alterations or attachments.

Revoking or changing a TOD deed

Any time before death, you can revoke or change a Kansas TOD deed by recording a new instrument. Under K.S.A. 59-3503 a revocation must be executed, acknowledged and recorded with the register of deeds where the land is, and the beneficiary's consent or notice is not needed. A later TOD deed automatically revokes all earlier beneficiary designations for the same interest.

One rule catches people out: a recorded TOD deed may not be revoked by a will. Simply denying a TOD in a will does not undo it. The Wyandotte register records revocations of TOD deeds and asks for the book and page number of the deed being revoked.

If the beneficiary dies before the owner

The gift lapses unless the deed names an alternate or the 2023 rule for surviving descendants applies. Under K.S.A. 59-3504(c), if a grantee beneficiary dies first and no alternate is named, the transfer to that beneficiary lapses. There is an exception. When the deed was not made contingent on the beneficiary surviving the owner and the beneficiary leaves at least one surviving child or other issue, the interest vests in those descendants per stirpes.

That exception comes from a 2023 amendment and applies to deeds filed of record on or after July 1, 2023 (K.S.A. 59-3504(e)). Older deeds follow the older rule. A court action to decide who succeeds goes through the probate code's descent procedure. A frequent mistake is naming one beneficiary and never planning for that person dying first.

Benefits and limits

A TOD deed skips probate for the house and keeps the owner in control, but it does not shield the property from debts or taxes.

  • Probate is avoided for the property, even if the same person is named in the will.
  • The beneficiary's own creditors cannot reach the property while the owner is alive, since the beneficiary has no interest yet.
  • It does not avoid the owner's creditors or state estate recovery.
  • It does not cause a Medicaid transfer penalty, since ownership does not move until death.
  • It does not replace a will. The rest of the estate still needs a plan.

It also costs far less than a probate. A transfer through a TOD deed is much cheaper than a transfer under a will or revocable trust, because it avoids court and clerical fees.

Selling a house that has a TOD deed

While the owner is alive, the owner can sell, because the deed gives the beneficiary no ownership. You still own your property and can sell it at any time. A sale by the owner is an ordinary deed transfer with the usual sales validation questionnaire and recording steps, which our Kansas quitclaim deed guide covers.

After the owner dies, the beneficiary holds title and can sell, subject to the existing mortgage and liens. Because the house passed outside probate, the beneficiary usually does not need a court appointment to sell it. Other assets in the estate may still be going through the court, so see our page on the Kansas probate process if the estate is open.

Beneficiaries who inherit a house they do not want to keep, or one that needs repairs, can ask us about an as-is cash sale. The title company will look at the recorded TOD deed, the death certificate and any open liens, so gather those first.

Titling a vehicle in TOD form

K.S.A. 59-3508 allows a motor vehicle to be titled in TOD form by naming a beneficiary on the certificate of title. This is handled through the county treasurer or tag office, usually at registration time, and must be done for each vehicle. It is a separate process from the real estate deed recorded with the register of deeds.

Checklist before you sign

Pull your current deed and confirm exactly how title is held. Decide on a beneficiary and an alternate. Have the new deed prepared, signed before a notary and recorded with the register of deeds in the county where the property sits. Keep a copy of the recorded deed with your other papers, and tell the person who will handle your estate where it is.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Is a TOD deed legal in Kansas?

Yes. Kansas authorizes transfer on death deeds in K.S.A. 59-3501 and following. The deed must be signed, acknowledged and recorded with the register of deeds in the county where the land lies before the owner dies.

Does the beneficiary have to sign a Kansas TOD deed?

No. K.S.A. 59-3501 and 59-3503 say the beneficiary's signature, consent or notice is not required while the owner is alive. The deed also needs no consideration.

Can I sell my house after recording a TOD deed?

Yes. The deed transfers nothing until your death, so you can sell the property, revoke the deed or change the beneficiary during your life.

Does a TOD deed avoid probate in Kansas?

It avoids probate for the property it covers. The beneficiary takes the house subject to liens, mortgages and state medical assistance claims, and the rest of the estate may still need probate.

What if my TOD beneficiary dies first?

The transfer lapses unless an alternate beneficiary is named. For deeds filed on or after July 1, 2023, surviving children or other issue of the beneficiary can take instead, unless the deed was made contingent on the beneficiary surviving the owner.

Does Kansas tax capital gains on a house sale?

Yes, when the gain is taxable federally. Your Kansas return begins with federal adjusted gross income, so whatever gain the IRS counts follows you onto the state form. K.S.A. 79-32,117 builds Kansas adjusted gross income from federal AGI with listed modifications, and a single rate schedule then covers taxable income. No special Kansas rate exists for capital gains.

Start with the federal question: is any of your profit taxable? Gain the IRS lets you exclude never enters federal AGI, so Kansas never sees it either.

Sale price and gain are different things. Gain is the amount realized minus your adjusted basis, and a loss on a personal residence can't be deducted (IRS Topic 409).

Federal home sale exclusion

A principal residence qualifies for an exclusion of up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 for joint filers, if you pass two tests (IRS Topic 701).

  • Ownership: you held title for at least 24 months during the 5 years ending on the sale date.
  • Use: you lived there for at least 24 months of that same 5 year window, though not necessarily the same months.
  • Married couples: one spouse can satisfy ownership, but each must satisfy use.
  • Back-to-back sales: the exclusion is generally unavailable if you used it on another home within the previous two years.
  • Reporting: a Form 1099-S in your mailbox means the sale goes on your return, even if every dollar of gain is excluded.

Service members, Foreign Service staff and intelligence community employees on qualified official extended duty can elect to pause the five year clock for up to 10 years.

Federal rates on gain you can't exclude

Under 2025 federal rules, long-term gain is mostly taxed at 15%, with 0% and 20% bands at the low and high ends. Owning the home longer than a year makes the gain long-term. A year or less makes it short-term and subject to ordinary income rates.

Filing status (2025)0% rate up to15% rate up to
Single$48,350$533,400

Head of household$64,750$566,700

The figures are taxable income cutoffs, and income above the 15% band is taxed at 20%. Depreciation on a former rental can trigger a 25% maximum rate on unrecaptured section 1250 gain, and high earners may owe the net investment income tax as well.

Kansas tax on the gain

Kansas uses a single schedule for taxable income. For tax year 2025, a single filer pays 5.2% on the first $23,000, then $1,196 plus 5.58% of the excess. Joint filers use $46,000 as the break point and $2,392 as the base. The 2025 standard deduction is $3,605 for single filers, $8,240 for joint filers, $4,120 for married filing separately and $6,180 for head of household.

Kansas has enacted further income tax rate cuts, so check the instruction booklet for the year you sell instead of relying on the 2025 figures.

Adjusting your Kansas basis

Kansas allows a subtraction where your Kansas adjusted basis is higher than your federal basis, limited to the gain included in federal AGI (K.S.A. 79-32,117(c)(iii)).

Basis starts with your purchase cost. Inherited property is different: IRS Publication 551 sets basis at market value on the day the owner died. Heirs who sell soon after often see little or no gain, so order an appraisal that fixes that value. Our page on Kansas estate and inheritance tax covers the inheritance side.

Payments spread over several years make the sale an installment sale, reported under the installment method unless you elect out. You can still use the home exclusion.

Living outside Kansas but owning a Kansas house

The gain is still a Kansas matter. K.S.A. 79-3276(a) allocates capital gains and losses from sales of Kansas real property to Kansas, and a nonresident owner is taxed on gains realized from the sale of property located in Kansas.

For estimated tax, a nonresident considers only Kansas-source income when testing the conditions. You must make payments if your expected Kansas tax after withholding and credits is $500 or more and your withholding may fall short of the smaller of 90% of this year's tax or 100% of last year's tax.

  • Voucher dates each year: April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15.
  • Payments go to Estimated Tax, Kansas Department of Revenue, PO Box 3506, Topeka, KS 66625-3506, or online through the Kansas payment portal.
  • The Department's taxpayer line is 785-368-8222.

Forms for reporting a Kansas house sale

Federally, the gain is worked out on Form 8949 and carried to Schedule D of Form 1040 when reporting is required. The closing agent's Form 1099-S forces a report even for fully excluded gain.

A personal-home loss gets no deduction. Other capital losses you hold can offset income only up to $3,000 a year ($1,500 if married filing separately), and the rest carries forward. A taxable gain can also call for federal estimated payments (see Publication 505).

Kansas starts from the federal return, so a mistake in the federal calculation repeats on the state return. Keep the closing disclosure, improvement receipts and exclusion worksheet together for as long as the return could be questioned.

A step-by-step check for sellers

  1. Confirm the house was your main home, and count the months you owned it and lived in it during the last five years.
  2. Find your basis: your purchase cost plus improvements, or the date-of-death value if you inherited.
  3. Subtract basis from what you will realize at closing to see the gain.
  4. Compare that gain with $250,000 or $500,000, depending on your filing status.
  5. If any gain is left, work out whether it is long-term, then expect it to flow into Kansas taxable income on the single schedule above.
  6. Keep the Form 1099-S and closing statement for your return.

Most owners who lived in the house for years and bought at a normal price stop at step four with nothing left to tax. Landlords, heirs who wait years to sell, and owners who moved out early are the ones who should look closely.

Planning before you accept an offer

Settle your basis and exclusion figures first. Those two numbers decide whether you owe anything. A cash buyer leaves the math alone, because the rules look at basis, ownership and use.

Pull together your original closing statement, improvement receipts, and any appraisal or tax record that supports a date-of-death value. A tax professional can say whether a December closing, or installment payments, moves the gain into a different tax year.

Pick your return preparer early. If you are near the edge of the 24 month tests, a few weeks of delay can change the answer, so count the days before signing a contract.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a special Kansas capital gains rate?

No. Gain flows into Kansas adjusted gross income from federal AGI and is taxed on the standard schedule, which for 2025 is 5.2% and 5.58%.

Do I owe Kansas tax if I exclude the gain on my federal return?

Generally no. Excluded gain stays out of federal AGI, the starting line for Kansas. A Form 1099-S still means you report the sale.

How long must I live in the house to use the exclusion?

Twenty-four months of ownership and 24 months of living there as your main home, both within the five years before closing. The months needn't match.

Does a nonresident owe Kansas tax on a Kansas house sale?

Yes. K.S.A. 79-3276(a) allocates gains from Kansas real property to Kansas, so nonresidents are taxed on them.

What is my basis if I inherited the house?

Usually the market value on the date the prior owner died (IRS Publication 551). Exceptions exist, so confirm with a tax professional.

How probate works in Kansas

Probate in Kansas runs through the district court. Its job is to prove a will, name someone to manage the estate, pay valid debts and pass what is left to the people entitled to it. Every probate proceeding is under the district court's authority, and juries are not used.

If the person left a will, it names an executor. With no will, the court appoints an administrator. Either one is personally responsible for handling the estate properly: notifying heirs and creditors, inventorying and protecting the assets, paying taxes and valid claims, and distributing the rest. Appointing an executor usually takes four to five weeks from the day the petition is filed, though no two estates run on the same schedule.

For someone who inherited a house, the practical point is simple. Until a personal representative has been appointed, nobody has clear authority to sign a sale contract for the estate. A person who deals with the dead owner's property without a formal court appointment can be held personally responsible for what they do.

Probate deadlines

Four dates matter most to a family thinking about selling an inherited house: the six-month window to file a will, the 30-day publication step, the four-month creditor period and the small estate ceiling of $75,000.

Main Kansas probate time limits and thresholds
StepRule
Filing a will for probate (K.S.A. 59-617)A will does not pass property unless a petition is filed within six months of the death
Publishing notice to creditors (K.S.A. 59-709)Petitioner gives notice within 30 days after filing, once a week for three consecutive weeks, in a county newspaper
Creditor claim window (K.S.A. 59-2239)Four months from first publication, or 30 days after actual notice to a known creditor if that is later
Small estate affidavit (K.S.A. 59-1507b)Personal property can move without letters when probate assets are $75,000 or less
Earliest closingAn estate with assets beyond allowances and debts cannot close before six months after death

The 30-day publication period is recent. A 2024 law (Senate Bill 379) lengthened it from 10 days to 30 days after the petition is filed, so older articles and forms may still show the shorter number.

Property that skips probate

Only property titled in the dead person's name alone, with no beneficiary or survivor rights attached, normally goes through probate. Several kinds of property bypass it:

  • Property held in joint tenancy with right of survivorship
  • Life insurance paid to a named beneficiary other than the estate
  • Bank accounts with a pay on death designation
  • Assets with transfer on death provisions, including securities, titled vehicles and real estate

The last item matters for houses. If the owner recorded a transfer on death deed before dying, the house passes to the named beneficiary outside the estate. Our guide to the Kansas transfer on death deed covers how those deeds work. If no such deed or survivorship title exists, the house is a probate asset.

Selling the house during probate

Yes, an executor can sell, and the route depends on the will. Under K.S.A. 59-1413, if a will authorizes the executor to sell property, the executor may use that power without an order of the district court, unless the will provides otherwise. The power cannot be used while a proceeding to contest the will or to probate a later will is pending.

A buyer in good faith who takes title under that power gets the real estate free of the creditors' liens and claims against the estate and the heirs. Those claims move to the sale proceeds. Tax liens are the exception, and the statute says the transfer does not affect them.

When the will gives no power of sale, or there is no will, the administrator petitions the court instead. K.S.A. 59-2303 lets the petition name a prospective purchaser and the proposed terms, ask the court to approve appraisers and ask it to confirm the deal. If the buyer is related to the fiduciary by blood or finances, the petition has to say so. If there is no relationship, the petition says that instead.

The court path also has a public auction option. Notice of an auction of real estate must run once a week for three consecutive weeks in a county newspaper, and the sale date falls no sooner than 10 days and no later than 30 days after the last publication (K.S.A. 59-2308). Many families prefer a negotiated private sale for that reason.

What a small estate affidavit covers

The small estate affidavit in K.S.A. 59-1507b covers personal property only, so it does not move title to a house. When a Kansas resident dies with probate assets of $75,000 or less, a successor can give a bank or other holder an affidavit and collect personal property without letters of administration. The 2024 amendment also lets the property go to a person claiming to be a successor, or as that successor directs.

Real estate needs a different step. When someone dies without a will and leaves only real estate, a determination of descent proceeding can be started any time six months after death, and it typically takes about 30 days. That proceeding gives the heirs a court record of who owns the house before they sell.

The Kansas courts run a self-help probate page that links the Judicial Council forms, including the small estates affidavit. Questions go to the local district court.

Costs and taxes on a Kansas estate

Fees for the executor and the lawyer are not fixed by law. They must reflect the fair value of the work compared with the size of the estate, and the probate court approves them. Court fees are set by law, and publication charges and a bond premium may be added.

Property tax keeps running while the estate is open. Kansas real estate tax is due in full by December 20, or in two halves, with the second half due May 10 of the next year (K.S.A. 79-2004). Unpaid amounts draw interest at the statutory rate plus five percentage points. A house that sits through a long probate can pick up a tax bill and interest before anyone sells it. Our Kansas property tax guide walks through the calendar.

A transfer on death deed does not avoid creditors. An executor should not prepare the estate's tax returns without a lawyer's help.

First steps for heirs who inherit a house

Protect the house, call a probate lawyer and gather the paperwork, in that order. Nothing should be done to disturb the dead person's property unless it is needed to keep it from being lost or destroyed. Contact a lawyer soon after the death, with the will in hand at the first meeting.

  • Locate the original will and note the date of death, since the six-month filing window starts there.
  • Find the recorded deed. Check whether it shows joint tenants or a transfer on death beneficiary.
  • List the mortgage, tax and utility accounts, and note the next property tax due date.
  • Ask the lawyer whether the will gives the executor a power of sale, since that changes whether a court order is needed.
  • Decide among the heirs who will sign, because every owner or the court-appointed representative must agree to a sale.

Where a cash sale fits

A cash purchase fits at the point where the personal representative has authority, and the sale proceeds then pass through the estate account to creditors and heirs. A cash buyer can close without waiting on a bank's loan approval, which removes one source of delay in an estate that already has court steps to finish.

We buy houses as-is, so an inherited property that needs repairs, has personal belongings left in it or sits vacant can still be considered. The title company handling the closing will want to see the court's appointment of the executor or administrator and, where the will grants no power of sale, the court's order. Ask the estate's lawyer which documents apply to your file before you sign anything.

Frequently asked questions

How long does probate take in Kansas?

There is no fixed length. Appointing an executor usually takes four to five weeks after filing, creditors have four months, and an estate with assets beyond allowances and debts cannot close before six months after the date of death. Many estates run longer.

Can I sell an inherited house in Kansas before probate is finished?

Sometimes. If the will gives the executor a power of sale, no court order is needed under K.S.A. 59-1413. Without that power, the administrator asks the district court for approval under K.S.A. 59-2303. Either way a court-appointed representative must exist first.

Does a small estate affidavit transfer a house in Kansas?

No. K.S.A. 59-1507b covers personal property when probate assets are $75,000 or less. Real estate needs probate or a determination of descent, unless a transfer on death deed or survivorship title already controls it.

How many days does a creditor have to file a claim?

Four months from the first publication of notice, or 30 days after actual notice to a known or reasonably ascertainable creditor if that is later (K.S.A. 59-2239). Claims presented after that are barred.

Do I need a lawyer for a Kansas probate?

Not every estate requires one, but it is wise to contact a lawyer soon after a death, and an executor should not prepare tax returns without a lawyer's guidance. This page is general information and not legal advice.
